title: God Creates the Heavens and the Earth
summary: By His word God forms and fills the earth in six evening-and-morning days, crowning His work with humanity made in His image.
historicalContext: Genesis 1 was first received by Israel, a people lately brought out of Egypt and soon to live beside Canaanites and within reach of Babylon, nations whose stories of origins were crowded with rival gods. In those stories the sea was a goddess, the sun and moon were deities, the sky was carved from a slain monster, and humans were fashioned to relieve the gods of drudgery. Moses answers that world without adopting its theology. One God, uncreated and unopposed, speaks, and everything else exists because He wills it. Water is only water, the sun and moon are lamps, the great sea creatures are His creatures, and human beings are honored as His image instead of being conscripted as servants of hungry gods. The chapter also lays the foundation of the week Israel would keep, a link the fourth commandment makes explicit (Exodus 20:11).
literaryContext: Together with 2:1–3, this chapter forms the opening movement of Genesis and of the whole Bible. Its elevated prose advances by repeated formulas—“And God said,” “and it was so,” “God saw that it was good,” “the evening and the morning were”—which give the account the cadence of an ordered report. Verse 1 states the subject; verse 2 describes an earth not yet formed or filled; verses 3–31 narrate six consecutive days. The first three days shape realms (light and darkness, sky and seas, land and plants), and the next three populate them (luminaries, birds and fish, land animals and humanity). The sixth day receives the most space and the strongest verdict, “very good.” The section reaches its goal in the seventh day, which God blesses and sanctifies, and it is joined to the following narrative by the heading of 2:4, “These are the generations of the heavens and of the earth.”
themes: God as sole and sovereign Creator
An earth formed and filled in six literal days
The goodness of the created world
Humanity made in the image of God

outline.title: The Creator and the Unformed Earth
outline.summary: God creates the heavens and the earth; the earth lies dark, empty, and covered with water while the Spirit hovers over it.

outline.title: Days One to Three: Realms Formed
outline.summary: By His word God brings light, separates the waters with the expanse, gathers the seas, raises dry land, and clothes it with plants.

outline.title: Days Four and Five: Lights, Seas, and Skies Filled
outline.summary: God appoints the luminaries to rule day and night and fills the waters and the air with creatures He blesses.

outline.title: Day Six: Land Creatures and Humanity
outline.summary: God makes the land animals, then creates man and woman in His image, blessing them with fruitfulness and dominion.

outline.title: Provision and the Verdict of “Very Good”
outline.summary: God assigns plant food to humans and animals and surveys the finished work of the six days as very good.

verses.bibleText: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The Bible opens with God. “In the beginning God” sets the Creator before every created thing and beyond the reach of time, space, and matter. All that follows in Scripture rests on this sentence. If God made all things, then all things belong to Him, depend on Him, and must finally answer to Him (Psalm 24:1; Revelation 4:11). The verse stands as a complete statement, the heading and summary of the chapter, and the verses after it unfold how the Creator brought this earth into order and life.

The Hebrew sentence is spare—seven words, with the name of God at its center. Some modern translations render the opening “When God began to create,” as though material already lay waiting. The traditional rendering remains the stronger reading. The ancient versions, the separating accent the Hebrew text places on the first word, and the short independent sentences that run through the chapter all point to an absolute beginning. Isaiah speaks of God “declaring the end from the beginning” (Isaiah 46:10), and Hebrews concludes that “the things which are seen were not made of things which do appear” (Hebrews 11:3). God alone is self-existent; everything else, in heaven or on earth, owes its being to Him.

The verb “created” is reserved in the Old Testament for divine activity. People make, shape, and build from what is at hand; only God creates in this sense. The verb never names a material, only a result, and it returns at decisive points of the account: the great sea creatures (v. 21), humanity (v. 27), and the summary of the whole work (2:3–4). “The heaven and the earth” pairs opposites to express everything that exists. Israel’s neighbors pictured the world emerging from conflict among gods or from the body of a defeated deity. Genesis allows no rival, no material independent of God, and no battle. God acts alone, freely, and without opposition.

The New Testament reads this verse in the light of Christ. John opens his Gospel with the same words, “In the beginning,” and identifies the Word who was with God and was God as the One through whom “all things were made” (John 1:1–3). Paul writes that by the Son “were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth” (Colossians 1:16). The Creator of Genesis 1 is the Redeemer of the Gospels. The God who brought a universe into being can also make a person new, and Scripture uses creation language for that work (Psalm 51:10; 2 Corinthians 5:17). To confess “In the beginning God” is to place every other beginning, including one’s own, in His hands.

wordNotes.explanation: The noun re’shit denotes the first point or opening part of something. Here, standing without a following noun and marked off by a separating accent, the phrase introduces the absolute start of the created order, not merely the first stage of an existing process. The Greek Old Testament renders it en archē, the very words with which John begins his Gospel to present the Word as already existing when that beginning came.

In this stem the verb always has God as its subject and never mentions the material out of which something comes. It stresses divine initiative and the bringing about of something new. The verb by itself does not prove creation from nothing; the context of an absolute beginning does. Elsewhere it describes God creating a clean heart and new heavens and a new earth, works only He can do.

verses.bibleText: And the earth was without form, and void; and darkness was upon the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The focus narrows from “the heaven and the earth” to “the earth.” Before God’s first spoken command the planet is described in three clauses: it was “without form, and void”; darkness lay over “the deep”; and the Spirit of God “moved upon the face of the waters.” The picture is of a world covered by water, unlit, and empty of life. It is not yet shaped for habitation or filled with inhabitants, and the six days that follow answer each lack in turn. Light will meet the darkness, separation will give shape, and living creatures will fill what was empty.

Some have read the verse as “the earth became waste and void,” imagining an earlier perfect world ruined by catastrophe—often linked with Satan’s fall—followed by long ages and a re-creation. The Hebrew does not support this. The sentence is a circumstantial description of the earth’s condition, using the ordinary form for what “was,” not the narrative form that would signal a fresh event after verse 1. Tohu wabohu describes something unformed and uninhabited, not something judged. When Isaiah says God “created it not in vain [tohu], he formed it to be inhabited” (Isaiah 45:18), he speaks of God’s purpose: the Creator did not leave the earth empty. Scripture gives no warrant for inserting a ruined former world or vast ages of death before the creation week, and the New Testament traces death to human sin (Romans 5:12). The text is also silent on how long the earth lay in this state, and silence is no invitation to speculate.

“The deep” translates tehom, the primeval ocean. Babylonian myth personified the sea as Tiamat, a hostile goddess split in two to make sky and earth. Genesis speaks of the deep with no personality, no rivalry, and no threat. It is water under the Creator’s control, awaiting His word.

Over those waters the Spirit of God was moving. Ruach can mean wind or breath, but “the Spirit of God” elsewhere in the Pentateuch is God’s own presence equipping and giving life (Exodus 31:3), and the verb pictures hovering, not a storm. The Spirit is present before the first word is spoken, ready to bring order and life. Psalm 104:30 links His sending with creatures being created, and the same Spirit later gives new birth (John 3:5–8). Christian readers rightly find here the first trace of the Godhead at work in creation, which the New Testament brings into full view.

wordNotes.term: תֹהוּ וָבֹהוּ (tohu wabohu) — without form, and void
wordNotes.explanation: The rhyming pair describes a state that is unformed and empty. Tohu on its own can mean a trackless waste or emptiness, and bohu occurs only alongside it. The phrase points to an earth not yet shaped for habitation and not yet populated. When Jeremiah uses it of a land under judgment, he borrows the language of this verse to picture creation running backward; he does not imply that the original condition was itself the product of judgment.

The participle describes continuing action: the Spirit was hovering. The same form of the verb appears only once more, where an eagle hovers over its young. The image suggests watchful, protective presence over the waters in preparation for what God is about to do, quite unlike a violent wind sweeping across them.

verses.bibleText: And God said, Let there be light: and there was light.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And God said” opens each day’s work and occurs ten times in the chapter. Creation proceeds by speech. The psalmist sums it up: “He spake, and it was done; he commanded, and it stood fast” (Psalm 33:9). No labor, struggle, or incantation stands between God’s will and its fulfillment. His word carries His power and accomplishes what He purposes (Isaiah 55:11). Speech is also a personal act, and from the first page God reveals Himself as One who wills, communicates, and acts with intention.

The first command is “Let there be light.” In Hebrew it is two words, yehi ’or, and the fulfillment echoes them: wayehi ’or, “and there was light.” The match between command and result is exact and immediate. Light comes first because every later work depends on it: plants will need it, creatures will see by it, and the rhythm of evening and morning requires it. That light appears before the sun is mentioned has puzzled some readers, yet the text is clear that God is the source of light and that He later appoints the luminaries to carry and govern it (vv. 14–18). The God who covers Himself “with light as with a garment” (Psalm 104:2) needed no sun to illuminate His world.

Scripture takes this moment as a pattern of redemption. Paul writes that “God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). John speaks of the Word in whom “was life; and the life was the light of men,” a light that the darkness has not overcome (John 1:4–5). The word that pierced the darkness over the deep still enters lives darkened by sin, confusion, or grief, and it is as effective there as it was on the first day. At the end of the story the city of God will need no sun, “for the glory of God did lighten it” (Revelation 21:23).

wordNotes.term: יְהִי אוֹר (yehi ’or) — Let there be light
wordNotes.explanation: The jussive yehi expresses a command addressed to what does not yet exist. The narrative answers with the matching form wayehi, “and there was,” so that the fulfillment repeats the command word for word. The Greek Old Testament preserves the pattern: genēthētō phōs, kai egeneto phōs. The construction stresses the immediacy and completeness of God’s effective word.

verses.bibleText: And God saw the light, that it was good: and God divided the light from the darkness.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
For the first time God evaluates what He has made: “God saw the light, that it was good.” The formula will recur through the chapter until the final “very good” of verse 31. God’s seeing is an assessment by the One whose plan is the standard, and the light does exactly what He intended. The Hebrew tov embraces more than usefulness; it includes what is pleasing and beautiful and, as the story unfolds, what is morally right. Creation works, and it also delights its Maker.

Here the object is named—God saw “the light”—where later days speak more generally of what He had done. The light itself is pronounced good. Darkness is not called good, and the chapter never says it was created; it is assigned a place. Scripture elsewhere affirms that God rules darkness as fully as light (Isaiah 45:7; Psalm 139:12), so the omission implies no rival power. It simply marks light as the first gift.

Then “God divided the light from the darkness.” Separation is one of the chapter’s key actions: light from darkness, waters from waters, day from night. Each thing receives its proper sphere. This orderly distinguishing stands in contrast to the separations sin will later bring—humanity from God, husband from wife, man from the ground. In the New Testament, light and darkness become moral categories. God “is light, and in him is no darkness at all” (1 John 1:5), and believers are called “out of darkness into his marvellous light” (1 Peter 2:9).

wordNotes.explanation: A broad term for what is pleasing, beneficial, and fitting. In this chapter it expresses God’s approval of each work as fulfilling His purpose. Its later use in “the tree of the knowledge of good and evil” shows that the word also carries moral weight, so the goodness of creation becomes the backdrop against which sin is understood.

The verb means to separate or distinguish, assigning things to their proper place. It recurs in verses 6, 7, 14, and 18. Later the law uses it for distinguishing holy from common and clean from unclean, and for God’s setting Israel apart from the nations, so the ordering work of creation becomes a pattern for holy living.

verses.bibleText: And God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night. And the evening and the morning were the first day.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
God names what He has divided: “God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night.” In the ancient world, naming expressed authority over what was named. God names day and night, heaven, earth, and seas, and afterward entrusts naming to Adam (2:19–20). By naming even the darkness, God shows that it lies within His rule and does not stand beside Him as a power of its own.

“And the evening and the morning were the first day.” The Hebrew reads, “and there was evening and there was morning, day one.” Yom, “day,” is used in this verse first for the period of light and then for the whole cycle of darkness and light. Joined to a number and framed by evening and morning, the word describes an ordinary day throughout the Old Testament. The refrain closes each of the six days, and the days are numbered in sequence. The most natural reading, and the one the rest of Scripture confirms, is that these were literal, consecutive days of about twenty-four hours.

The fourth commandment settles the question. God grounds Israel’s week on the creation week: “For in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them is, and rested the seventh day” (Exodus 20:11). Israel’s six working days and its Sabbath were ordinary days, and the command draws its force from that correspondence. Readings that stretch each day into a long age, or that treat the days as a literary frame only, generally arise from the effort to fit the text to theories of slow development over vast time, and they dissolve the link the commandment makes. Peter’s remark that “one day is with the Lord as a thousand years” (2 Peter 3:8) concerns God’s patience in fulfilling His promises, and the same verse adds that a thousand years are “as one day.” Those who hold other views often do so sincerely, but the wording of Genesis and of the law points to real days.

Evening comes before morning. Israel reckoned days from sunset to sunset (Leviticus 23:32), and the order of the refrain fits that reckoning. Each creation day begins in darkness and moves into light, mirroring the movement of the whole chapter from a dark, empty deep toward a world full of life. The pattern carries a note of hope: with God, darkness is never the final word.

wordNotes.term: וַיְהִי־עֶרֶב וַיְהִי־בֹקֶר יוֹם אֶחָד (wayehi-‘erev wayehi-voqer yom ’echad) — the evening and the morning were the first day
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “there was evening and there was morning, day one.” The cardinal “one,” where the later days use ordinals, may present this as the first unit of a series that defines what a day is. Daniel uses the compound “evening-morning” as a unit of time, and Paul uses a single Greek word for a full night-and-day period. The formula marks a complete, ordinary day.

The word can denote daylight, as in the first half of this verse, a full day, or, in phrases such as “in the day that,” a more general time. Context decides. When yom is joined to a number and framed by evening and morning, as throughout Genesis 1, it refers to a normal day, which is how the fourth commandment and the Sabbath sign read it.

verses.bibleText: And God said, Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The second day opens as the first did, with God’s word: “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters.” On the first day God ordered time; now He orders space. The waters that covered the earth are parted into two bodies with an open expanse between them. This creates the room in which birds will fly and beneath which land will soon appear, and it prepares the sky that the fifth day will fill.

The English “firmament” comes from the Latin firmamentum, which suggested something solid. The Hebrew raqia‘ comes from a verb meaning to spread out or beat out, and Scripture uses related imagery freely: God stretches out the heavens “like a curtain” (Psalm 104:2), and Elihu likens the sky to a cast mirror (Job 37:18). Such language describes the heavens as they appear to an observer. The passage does not teach that Israel pictured a metal dome; the same expanse is where birds fly (v. 20) and where the lights are set (v. 14). The best sense is the open sky spread above the earth.

The expanse exists to separate: “let it divide the waters from the waters.” What the upper waters were, the text does not explain; water held aloft as cloud and vapor is the most natural understanding, and Psalm 148:4 still summons the “waters that be above the heavens” to praise the Lord. The emphasis falls on God’s authority over the waters. He sets their bounds, and they keep the places He assigns them (Proverbs 8:27–29).

wordNotes.explanation: The noun derives from a verb meaning to spread out, whether by hammering, as with metal, or by stretching. It names what has been spread out—here the expanse of the sky. Its later uses in poetry and vision are descriptive, not technical. In this chapter birds fly across the face of the firmament and the luminaries are set in it, so the word refers to the visible heavens above the earth.

verses.bibleText: And God made the firmament, and divided the waters which were under the firmament from the waters which were above the firmament: and it was so.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Command is followed by action: “God made the firmament, and divided the waters which were under the firmament from the waters which were above the firmament.” The chapter alternates between reports of what God said and reports of what God did. Apart from light, nothing is described as appearing by command alone; the word is matched by God’s own working (vv. 16, 21, 25, 27). The narrative thus keeps the Creator from seeming remote. He speaks with authority and acts with personal involvement.

“And it was so” confirms that the result corresponded to the word. Here it stands after the report of the deed, as if to say that the work matched the command in every detail. Babylonian myth pictured the sky formed from half of a slain goddess’s body, with bars and guards posted to keep her waters from bursting out. Genesis has no corpse, no guards, and no menace. God made the expanse, and the waters stay where He puts them. The same word still upholds “all things” (Hebrews 1:3).

wordNotes.explanation: Literally “and it was thus.” The phrase confirms that what God commanded came about exactly as He spoke. In this chapter it usually follows the command (vv. 9, 11, 15, 24, 30); here it follows the account of God’s action, underscoring that word and deed coincide.

verses.bibleText: And God called the firmament Heaven. And the evening and the morning were the second day.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
God names the expanse “Heaven.” The Hebrew shamayim serves both for the sky where birds fly and clouds gather and for the dwelling of God; Solomon speaks of “the heaven and heaven of heavens” (1 Kings 8:27). Here it denotes the visible sky, and even that points beyond itself, for the heavens “declare the glory of God” (Psalm 19:1). The sky God named here also became the direction of prayer for His people: “Unto thee lift I up mine eyes, O thou that dwellest in the heavens” (Psalm 123:1).

The second day alone lacks the words “it was good.” The omission implies no defect. The separation of the waters is finished only on the third day, when the lower waters are gathered and dry land appears, and the verdict waits until that work is whole (v. 10). The day closes with the familiar refrain, “the evening and the morning were the second day,” another ordinary day in the creation week.

wordNotes.explanation: A noun with plural form used for the sky, for the realm of the heavenly bodies, and for the dwelling of God. Context determines the sense. Here God gives the name to the atmospheric expanse He has just made. In the pairing “heaven and earth” the same word helps express the whole created order.

verses.bibleText: And God said, Let the waters under the heaven be gathered together unto one place, and let the dry land appear: and it was so.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
On the third day God addresses the waters below the sky: “Let the waters under the heaven be gathered together unto one place, and let the dry land appear.” The work is twofold—the waters are concentrated and the land emerges. Until now the earth has been a world of water; now it gains a shoreline. The text narrates the land’s appearing more than its formation, as the waters withdraw to the basins God assigns.

Psalm 104 describes the same moment in poetry: the waters stood above the mountains, fled at God’s rebuke, and went down to the place He founded for them, behind a boundary they may not cross (Psalm 104:6–9). Job hears God ask who “shut up the sea with doors” and said, “Hitherto shalt thou come, but no further” (Job 38:8–11). The restraint of the sea is an act of kindness. A habitable world requires land kept safe from the deep.

That boundary will be lifted for a time in the flood, when “the fountains of the great deep” are broken up and the waters again cover the earth (7:11, 19). Peter recalls both events together: the earth “standing out of the water and in the water” by God’s word, and the world that then was “overflowed with water” (2 Peter 3:5–6). The God who set the bounds can also remove them, and His word governs both creation and judgment.

wordNotes.explanation: From a verb meaning to be dry, the word describes ground no longer covered by water. It reappears when Israel crosses the Red Sea and the Jordan on dry ground, so the deliverance at the sea echoes the third day: God again divides the waters and makes a path of dry land for His people.

verses.bibleText: And God called the dry land Earth; and the gathering together of the waters called he Seas: and God saw that it was good.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
God names the dry land “Earth” and the gathered waters “Seas.” The word for earth, ’erets, has been used since verse 1 for the planet as a whole; now it also names the land in particular, the home about to be prepared for creatures and people. This is the last act of divine naming in the chapter. From here on God creates without naming, and the privilege of naming living creatures will be given to Adam (2:19–20).

“And God saw that it was good.” The verdict held back on the second day is now given, because the separation of the waters is complete. Bare hills and empty valleys might not have looked good to us, but God sees each stage in relation to what He intends, and the land is good because it is ready for what comes next. The psalmist turns the fact into worship: “The sea is his, and he made it: and his hands formed the dry land. O come, let us worship and bow down” (Psalm 95:5–6).

wordNotes.explanation: The plural of yam, “sea.” In Canaanite myth Yam was a sea god and an enemy of Baal. Genesis uses the ordinary noun for waters gathered into one place and named by God, so the seas appear as created waters under His authority, with no will or divinity of their own.

verses.bibleText: And God said, Let the earth bring forth grass, the herb yielding seed, and the fruit tree yielding fruit after his kind, whose seed is in itself, upon the earth: and it was so.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The third day has a second work. God commands, “Let the earth bring forth grass, the herb yielding seed, and the fruit tree yielding fruit after his kind.” The bare land is to be clothed. Three kinds of vegetation are named: tender green growth, seed-bearing plants, and fruit trees whose seed lies within the fruit. Whether the first is a heading for the other two or a separate class, the sweep runs from meadow to orchard. Verses 29–30 will reveal the purpose: these plants are food for humans and animals alike.

“Let the earth bring forth” gives no creative power to the soil. In surrounding cultures the earth and its fertility were worshipped, and harvests were sought through rites honoring gods of rain and ground. Genesis grants the earth no divinity. The ground produces because God commands it, and its fruitfulness remains His gift (Psalm 65:9–13; Acts 14:17).

Each plant is made with its seed “in itself, upon the earth.” From the first moment, God built into living things the capacity to reproduce. The Creator makes a world that continues; what He begins by His word He sustains through the processes He appoints. The phrase also implies maturity. The trees bear fruit on the day they appear, and nothing suggests seedlings slowly growing over ages. The garden Adam will tend is already stocked with trees “pleasant to the sight, and good for food” (2:9).

Jesus later drew on seed and fruit to teach about the kingdom and the heart. A good tree bears good fruit, and the word received in an honest heart yields a harvest (Matthew 7:17; Luke 8:15). The order of the third day stands behind such teaching: life reproduces according to its nature.

wordNotes.term: דֶּשֶׁא, עֵשֶׂב, עֵץ פְּרִי (deshe’, ‘esev, ‘ets peri) — grass, herb, fruit tree
wordNotes.explanation: Deshe’ refers to fresh green growth; ‘esev to plants, especially those bearing seed, such as grains and vegetables; ‘ets peri to fruit-bearing trees. The distinction between plants with exposed seed and trees with seed enclosed in fruit anticipates the two kinds of food assigned to humanity in verse 29.

verses.bibleText: And the earth brought forth grass, and herb yielding seed after his kind, and the tree yielding fruit, whose seed was in itself, after his kind: and God saw that it was good.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The fulfillment repeats the command almost word for word: “the earth brought forth grass, and herb yielding seed after his kind, and the tree yielding fruit, whose seed was in itself, after his kind.” The echo is deliberate. What God said is exactly what happened, and the earth responded at once. The narrative records no delay, no trial and error, and no gradual emergence.

“After his kind” occurs ten times in the chapter. It refers to the varied groups of plants and animals God made, each reproducing its own kind. The Hebrew min is a broad category and is not identical with the modern term “species,” so the text allows for variety within each kind. It does, however, stand against the idea that all living things descended from a single ancestor by unguided change. The kinds were distinct from the beginning because God made them so.

“And God saw that it was good.” The second verdict of the third day marks the completion of the habitable land. Paul’s reasoning about the resurrection body later draws on this order: “God giveth it a body as it hath pleased him, and to every seed his own body” (1 Corinthians 15:38).

wordNotes.explanation: From min, “kind” or “sort.” The term groups living things by type and recurs in the flood narrative and in the food laws that distinguish clean and unclean animals. It is a broad classification and should not be equated precisely with modern biological species, though it affirms that God established distinct kinds that reproduce after their own pattern.

verses.bibleText: And the evening and the morning were the third day.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The refrain closes the third day: “the evening and the morning were the third day.” The first half of the creation week is complete. Light and darkness, sky and sea, land and plants are in place—the three great realms of the earth have been formed.

The next three days will fill them in corresponding order. The third day is also the first with two distinct works and two verdicts of “good,” a pattern the sixth day will repeat on a larger scale. Like the others, it is counted in sequence and bounded by evening and morning, an ordinary day within an ordinary week.

wordNotes.explanation: The ordinal number, used here as for each day after the first. Throughout the Old Testament, numbered days in sequence refer to ordinary days, as in the third day of Abraham’s journey to Moriah or of Israel’s preparation at Sinai.

verses.bibleText: And God said, Let there be lights in the firmament of the heaven to divide the day from the night; and let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and years:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The fourth day corresponds to the first. Light was created on day one; now God appoints “lights in the firmament of the heaven” to bear and distribute it. The word me’orot means light-bearers or lamps, and outside this chapter the Pentateuch uses it for the lampstand that lit the tabernacle (Exodus 25:6; Numbers 4:9). The heavens are being furnished like a sanctuary, with lamps set in place by God.

Their purposes are spelled out more fully than for anything made so far. They are “to divide the day from the night,” taking up the work God Himself performed on day one (v. 4). They are “for signs,” markers through which God may speak, as when the sun stood still for Joshua or was darkened at the crucifixion (Joshua 10:12–13; Matthew 27:45); Jesus names signs “in the sun, and in the moon, and in the stars” among the events that precede His return (Luke 21:25). They are “for seasons,” the appointed times by which Israel’s annual feasts would be reckoned (Psalm 104:19; Leviticus 23:4). And they are “for days, and years,” the measures of every calendar.

One measure is missing: the week. Days, months, and years follow the movements of earth, moon, and sun, but the seven-day week rests on no astronomical cycle. It comes from God’s own creation week and His rest on the seventh day (2:2–3; Exodus 20:11). The Sabbath is fixed by the word of God, independent of the motions of the heavens.

These lights serve; they do not govern human destinies. Israel’s neighbors worshipped sun, moon, and stars and searched their movements for omens. Scripture forbids both practices (Deuteronomy 4:19; Isaiah 47:13–14; Jeremiah 10:2). The heavenly bodies are signs in God’s hand, never gods to be consulted, and the Creator alone directs the course of history.

wordNotes.explanation: A noun formed from ’or, “light,” with a prefix that often marks an instrument or place: a light-holder or lamp. Apart from this passage the Pentateuch uses it for the sanctuary lampstand and the oil that fed it. The word stresses function; the sun and moon are lamps God has made and hung in place.

From a verb meaning to appoint, the word denotes fixed times and meetings. It is the term for the “feasts of the LORD,” the appointed assemblies of Israel’s year, and the tabernacle is the “tent of meeting” from the same root. The heavenly lights mark the calendar by which those annual times were set.

verses.bibleText: And let them be for lights in the firmament of the heaven to give light upon the earth: and it was so.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And let them be for lights in the firmament of the heaven to give light upon the earth.” The third purpose is the most basic: to shine on the earth. The verse looks down from the sky to the ground. The lights are described from the standpoint of those who will live beneath them, not in terms of their own size or distance. Genesis views the cosmos from the earth and its future inhabitants, and the heavens are presented as serving that home.

“And it was so.” The arrangement God commanded was established, and it has continued. Jeremiah appeals to the fixed order of sun, moon, and stars as a pledge of God’s faithfulness: only if those ordinances fail will Israel cease to be a nation before Him (Jeremiah 31:35–36). Each sunrise testifies that the Creator keeps His word. James calls Him “the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning” (James 1:17).

wordNotes.explanation: The causative form of the verb “to be light,” meaning to shine upon or illuminate. Elsewhere God Himself gives light by the pillar of fire and by the shining of His face in blessing; the lamps of heaven do in a lesser way what God does in fullness.

verses.bibleText: And God made two great lights; the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night: he made the stars also.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Now the action: “God made two great lights; the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night.” The sun and moon go unnamed. The ordinary Hebrew words, shemesh and yareach, matched the names of deities across the ancient Near East—Shamash, the Mesopotamian sun god, and Yarikh, a moon god of Canaan. Genesis describes them only by size and function. They are great lights and nothing more.

Even their “rule” is assigned. They govern day and night only by marking and regulating them, as officials appointed by a king. Psalm 136 counts them among the works of God’s enduring love: He made “the sun to rule by day . . . the moon and stars to rule by night: for his mercy endureth for ever” (Psalm 136:8–9).

“He made the stars also.” In Hebrew the phrase is simply “and the stars,” attached almost in passing. In Babylonian myth the stars were great gods, set first among the heavenly bodies; Genesis dismisses them in a word. Whether the stars were brought into being during this week or are mentioned because they too are God’s handiwork, the text does not pause to say, and restraint is wise where Scripture is brief. Its point is plain: every light in the sky, however vast, owes its existence to God. Isaiah presses the lesson: “Lift up your eyes on high, and behold who hath created these things, that bringeth out their host by number: he calleth them all by names” (Isaiah 40:26).

Scripture also uses these lights to speak of Christ. Malachi foretells the “Sun of righteousness” arising “with healing in his wings” (Malachi 4:2), and Jesus calls Himself “the bright and morning star” (Revelation 22:16). The created lights point to the uncreated One who gives light to all.

wordNotes.term: הַמָּאֹר הַגָּדֹל (hamma’or haggadol) — the greater light
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “the great light,” with the comparison supplied by context. Using a descriptive title in place of the usual words for sun and moon keeps attention on their function and strips away any association with the sun and moon gods of Israel’s neighbors, whose worship the law later forbids.

The common word for stars, added briefly at the end of the sentence. Elsewhere the stars illustrate the countless descendants promised to Abraham and the unsearchable power of the God who counts and names them; for His people they are never objects of worship.

verses.bibleText: And God set them in the firmament of the heaven to give light upon the earth,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And God set them in the firmament of the heaven to give light upon the earth.” The verb is the ordinary Hebrew word for giving or placing. God positions the lights as a householder sets lamps where they are needed, and their location in the expanse is described as it appears from below.

The verse repeats a purpose already stated in verse 15. The repetition belongs to a deliberate pattern: the functions announced in verses 14–15 are restated in reverse order in verses 17–18, framing the section and pressing home that the heavenly bodies exist to serve. Psalm 8 draws the human conclusion. Considering “the moon and the stars, which thou hast ordained,” David marvels that God is mindful of mankind at all (Psalm 8:3–4). The lights were placed for those who would live on the earth, and the God who set them there attends to each of those people.

wordNotes.explanation: From natan, “to give, put, set.” The same verb describes God setting His bow in the cloud after the flood and putting His words in a prophet’s mouth. It expresses purposeful appointment by the Creator.

verses.bibleText: And to rule over the day and over the night, and to divide the light from the darkness: and God saw that it was good.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And to rule over the day and over the night, and to divide the light from the darkness.” The last phrase deliberately echoes verse 4, where God Himself “divided the light from the darkness.” What God did directly on the first day He now does through appointed means. The pattern runs through Scripture: God works through what He has made, while the power and the authority remain His.

The word “rule” anticipates what will be said of humanity. The luminaries govern the times; human beings will be given dominion over living creatures (v. 26). Both rule by delegation. When the creature forgets that its rule is borrowed, worship goes astray. Paul describes those who “worshipped and served the creature more than the Creator” (Romans 1:25), and Moses warns Israel against being drawn away to bow before the host of heaven (Deuteronomy 4:19).

“And God saw that it was good.” The heavenly lights fulfill their purpose with unfailing regularity. Their faithfulness to the order God set becomes in Scripture a picture of His own constancy and a rebuke to human fickleness (Psalm 89:37).

wordNotes.explanation: From mashal, “to rule, govern.” Here it describes regulation, not tyranny: the lights mark and order the times. The same verb is used of God’s kingdom ruling over all and, in Micah, of the coming Ruler who would go forth from Bethlehem.

verses.bibleText: And the evening and the morning were the fourth day.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the evening and the morning were the fourth day.” The refrain closes another ordinary day, the first in which sun and moon mark evening and morning.

The wording is identical to that of the three days before, which shows that the days preceding the luminaries were of the same kind as those after them. The fourth day thus binds the week into one continuous sequence: the light of the first three days and the sunlight of the last three measure the same kind of day.

wordNotes.explanation: The ordinal from the number four. It continues the unbroken count of days, each closed by the same refrain, so that no day in the sequence stands apart as a different kind of period.

verses.bibleText: And God said, Let the waters bring forth abundantly the moving creature that hath life, and fowl that may fly above the earth in the open firmament of heaven.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The fifth day fills the realms prepared on the second. God commands, “Let the waters bring forth abundantly the moving creature that hath life, and fowl that may fly above the earth in the open firmament of heaven.” The Hebrew is vivid: “Let the waters swarm with swarms of living creatures.” The seas are to teem with life from the smallest organisms to the largest. The language implies abundance—many creatures in great variety—rather than a lone pair of each.

The phrase “creature that hath life” is nefesh chayyah, “living being.” It is the first appearance of nefesh in Scripture, and it is applied to creatures of the sea. The same expression later describes animals on land (v. 24) and the man formed from dust when God breathes into him (2:7). Nefesh marks a breathing, animate creature, set apart from plants. It does not by itself denote an immortal part within; it describes the whole living being.

The King James wording can leave the impression that birds came from the waters. The Hebrew more naturally reads, that birds are to fly over the land, across the open expanse, and 2:19 says the birds were formed “out of the ground.” The waters swarm; the birds fill the expanse above.

With living creatures come motion, sound, and a new kind of beauty. Jesus pointed to the birds as evidence of the Father’s care: they neither sow nor reap, “yet your heavenly Father feedeth them” (Matthew 6:26). The God who filled the air with wings still notices each sparrow that falls (Matthew 10:29).

wordNotes.term: נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה (nefesh chayyah) — the moving creature that hath life
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “living being” or “living creature.” Nefesh denotes a breathing creature, the self as a living whole, and Scripture applies it to sea creatures before it applies it to humans. When the same phrase describes Adam in 2:7, it identifies him as a living being; it does not assign him a separate immortal entity that animals lack.

wordNotes.term: יִשְׁרְצוּ הַמַּיִם שֶׁרֶץ (yishretsu hammayim sherets) — let the waters bring forth abundantly
wordNotes.explanation: The verb and its related noun describe swarming or teeming, the movement of creatures in great numbers. After the flood God repeats the command that living things should “breed abundantly in the earth,” and Exodus uses the verb for Israel’s rapid increase in Egypt.

verses.bibleText: And God created great whales, and every living creature that moveth, which the waters brought forth abundantly, after their kind, and every winged fowl after his kind: and God saw that it was good.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And God created great whales.” For the first time since verse 1 the verb bara’ appears, for something new enters the world: animal life. The text singles out the tanninim, “great sea creatures,” before naming the smaller creatures of the water and the birds. “Whales” is too narrow a rendering; the word covers large creatures of the sea, and elsewhere it is used of serpents and of the crocodile-like monster that represents Egypt (Exodus 7:9; Ezekiel 29:3).

The choice is pointed. In Canaanite poetry the tannin was a chaos monster that the storm god had to subdue, and Israel’s neighbors told of battles between gods and sea dragons at the world’s origin. Later poets in Israel borrow such imagery to celebrate God’s triumph over proud nations (Psalm 74:13; Isaiah 51:9). Genesis tells of no battle at all. The greatest creatures of the deep are simply creatures, made by God on the fifth day and pronounced good. Psalm 104:26 even pictures Leviathan as formed to play in the sea. What others feared as a rival god appears here as part of the Creator’s handiwork.

The verse goes on to survey “every living creature that moveth, which the waters brought forth abundantly, after their kind, and every winged fowl after his kind.” The phrase “after their kind” is repeated for the creatures of the sea and for the birds. God establishes order within abundance. The variety of marine and bird life reflects intentional design, and each group reproduces within its own pattern.

“And God saw that it was good.” For the first time the earth holds creatures that move, feed, and sing. Psalm 148 calls “dragons, and all deeps” together with “flying fowl” to praise the Lord (Psalm 148:7, 10). Every creature, from the giant of the deep to the smallest bird, exists to display its Maker’s glory.

wordNotes.explanation: Tannin can mean a serpent, a large reptile, or a great sea creature, and in poetry it can serve as an image of hostile powers. Here, with the adjective “great,” it names the largest creatures of the sea. Their mention immediately after “God created” removes any thought that they were rival powers; they are made, not divine.

verses.bibleText: And God blessed them, saying, Be fruitful, and multiply, and fill the waters in the seas, and let fowl multiply in the earth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And God blessed them, saying, Be fruitful, and multiply.” For the first time in Scripture God blesses, and the first recipients are fish and birds. The blessing is tied to life’s capacity to continue: the creatures are to be fruitful, increase, and fill the waters and the earth. Light, sky, land, and plants were pronounced good; living creatures are pronounced good and also blessed.

God’s blessing is more than a kind wish. It is His effective word conferring power and well-being. In the ancient world fertility was sought from gods and goddesses through ritual. Genesis teaches that fruitfulness is the gift of the one Creator, given freely from the start. No rite is needed to secure it, and no other power controls it.

Blessing becomes one of the great words of Genesis. It is spoken over the first humans (v. 28), renewed to Noah after the flood (9:1), and promised to Abraham, through whom “all families of the earth” will be blessed (12:3). That promise reaches its fulfillment in Christ, through whom “the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles” (Galatians 3:14). The first blessing on the fifth day begins a thread that runs to the cross and beyond.

Here God addresses His creatures for the first time, though they cannot answer. With humanity He will speak in a fuller way, directly “unto them” (v. 28).

wordNotes.explanation: From barakh, “to bless.” When God blesses, He bestows life, fruitfulness, and well-being by His word. The verb occurs more often in Genesis than in any other book of the Old Testament and links creation with the promises later given to the patriarchs.

wordNotes.term: פְּרוּ וּרְבוּ (peru urevu) — Be fruitful, and multiply
wordNotes.explanation: Two imperatives that together command abundant increase. The pair recurs for humanity, for Noah, and for Jacob, and Exodus reports that Israel “were fruitful, and increased abundantly” in Egypt, evidence that the creation blessing was at work in God’s people.

verses.bibleText: And the evening and the morning were the fifth day.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the evening and the morning were the fifth day.” The refrain completes a day marked by abundance. The seas and skies, empty since the second day, are now filled with moving, living creatures that have received God’s first blessing.

With the close of this day the narrative stands one day from its climax. Each day so far has added a layer of order and life, and the pattern of forming and filling is nearly complete. The days are still counted one by one and bounded by the same evening and morning, moving steadily toward the sixth day, when the Creator will make the creature able to answer Him in worship.

wordNotes.explanation: The ordinal from the number five. As with the other days, the number joined to the evening-and-morning formula marks one day in a continuous series of six working days followed by a seventh day of rest.

verses.bibleText: And God said, Let the earth bring forth the living creature after his kind, cattle, and creeping thing, and beast of the earth after his kind: and it was so.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The sixth day, like the third, holds two works. First God addresses the land: “Let the earth bring forth the living creature after his kind, cattle, and creeping thing, and beast of the earth after his kind.” The dry land of the third day now receives its inhabitants. Three groups are named: “cattle,” the larger animals suited to life alongside people; “creeping thing,” small creatures that move close to the ground; and “beast of the earth,” wild animals that roam freely. Together they cover the animal life of the land.

As with the plants, “let the earth bring forth” does not make the ground a source of life in itself. Scripture knows nothing of life arising spontaneously from matter. The earth produces because God speaks, and 2:19 explains that “out of the ground the LORD God formed every beast of the field.” The animals share with humanity a body formed from the earth, and they share the designation “living creature.” The kinship is real, yet the verses that follow will reveal the decisive difference.

Domestic animals are distinguished from wild ones even at creation, though no hostility yet exists among them or toward people. Isaiah’s picture of the restored earth, where “the wolf also shall dwell with the lamb,” recalls this original peace (Isaiah 11:6–9).

wordNotes.explanation: Usually the larger four-footed animals, especially those living alongside people, such as herds and flocks; in some contexts it covers land animals in general. The word appears often in the laws concerning offerings and clean animals, where God’s instructions distinguish among the creatures He made.

An old, poetic form meaning “living thing of the land,” used for wild animals that roam freely, as distinct from domestic cattle. The same archaic form reappears in poetry, as when God claims “every beast of the forest” as His own.

verses.bibleText: And God made the beast of the earth after his kind, and cattle after their kind, and every thing that creepeth upon the earth after his kind: and God saw that it was good.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The fulfillment follows: “God made the beast of the earth after his kind, and cattle after their kind, and every thing that creepeth upon the earth after his kind.” The order of the three groups is reversed from the previous verse, a common Hebrew way of rounding off a statement. “Made” translates ‘asah, used throughout the chapter alongside bara’; God both speaks and works.

“After his kind” appears again for each group. The animals of the land, like the plants and sea creatures, belong to distinct kinds established by the Creator, and their diversity reflects design. Jesus reasoned from such order: “Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?” (Matthew 7:16).

“And God saw that it was good.” The verdict closes the account of the animals, and the narrative turns at once to its climax. The repeated “good” after each stage builds anticipation. Everything is ready—light, sky, seas, land, plants, luminaries, and creatures in every realm. The stage is set for the one creature who will be made in the image of God.

wordNotes.explanation: From ‘asah, a common verb for making or doing. In this chapter it alternates with bara’ without sharp contrast, since both describe God’s work (compare v. 26 with v. 27). The fourth commandment uses ‘asah to sum up the six days: “in six days the LORD made heaven and earth.”

verses.bibleText: And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The account slows and changes tone. Until now each work has begun with an impersonal command, “Let there be” or “Let the earth bring forth.” Now God speaks in the first person plural: “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness.” The shift signals that what follows is the summit of the week’s work. Humanity is introduced by divine deliberation.

Who is addressed in “us”? Some take it as a plural of majesty, others as God speaking to the angels of His court. Neither fits well. Scripture never presents angels as sharing in creation, and the next verse says plainly that God created man “in his own image.” The plural is best read as the speech of One who is plural within Himself. The Spirit of God has already appeared in verse 2, and the New Testament reveals the Son as the One through whom all things were made (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16; Hebrews 1:2). Later revelation supplies the vocabulary; the text already sets down the pattern of one God who speaks as “us.” The singular “his own image” in verse 27 guards God’s unity; the plural “us” discloses fellowship within the Godhead.

“Image” and “likeness” together express that humanity both resembles God and represents Him. Neither is defined here, and attempts to confine the image to one faculty—reason, conscience, or spirit alone—fall short. The whole person, body, mind, and moral nature, was made to reflect the Maker. In the ancient world kings set up statues of themselves to mark their authority in distant provinces, and a king might be called the image of a god. Genesis extends that dignity to every human being. All people, not rulers only, stand on earth as God’s representatives.

For that reason the image is joined at once to rule: “let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth.” The verb radah is used of kings and masters, and the law warns that such rule must not be harsh (Leviticus 25:43). Human dominion is stewardship under God, exercised in His character and for the good of what is ruled. Psalm 8 marvels at the honor: God made man “to have dominion over the works of thy hands” (Psalm 8:6).

Hebrews applies that psalm to Jesus, the true Man who fulfills humanity’s calling where Adam failed (Hebrews 2:6–9). Christ is “the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15), and through Him the image marred by sin is renewed in believers “after the image of him that created him” (Colossians 3:10).

wordNotes.term: נַעֲשֶׂה אָדָם (na‘aseh ’adam) — Let us make man
wordNotes.explanation: The cohortative “let us make” breaks the chapter’s pattern of third-person commands and expresses resolve within the speaker. ’Adam is collective here, “humankind,” as the plural “let them have dominion” shows; it later becomes the personal name of the first man. Plural divine speech recurs in later scenes of divine deliberation.

Tselem often denotes a physical figure or statue; demut denotes resemblance, from a verb meaning to be like. Used together they describe a creature who both resembles and represents God. The pair reappears when Adam fathers Seth “in his own likeness, after his image,” a family resemblance passed on. The Greek Old Testament renders them eikōn and homoiōsis, terms echoed when the New Testament calls Christ the image of God and speaks of people made after God’s likeness.

verses.bibleText: So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The fulfillment is told in three lines of poetry, the first in the Bible: “So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.” The verb bara’ occurs three times in this one verse. The narrator could hardly stress the point more: humanity is a new creation of God, distinct in kind from all that came before. The repetition gives the verse the force of a solemn proclamation.

The singular “his own image” follows the plural “our image” of verse 26. God is one even as He speaks as “us,” and the human creature reflects that one God. The image is neither divided among many deities nor shared with angels; it is the image of the living God.

The third line moves from the singular “him” to the plural “them.” The image of God is borne fully by both man and woman. Neither is more in God’s image than the other, and both receive the blessing and the commission that follow (v. 28). Sexual distinction belongs to God’s good design from the start; it is neither a later development nor a defect. Unlike the animals, humanity is not described “after his kind” but as male and female, a pairing that prepares for the fuller account of marriage in 2:18–25.

Jesus appealed to this verse when questioned about divorce: “Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female?” He joined it to 2:24 and concluded, “What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder” (Matthew 19:4–6). The Creator’s design at the beginning remains the standard for marriage. Paul reflects the same verse when he declares that in Christ “there is neither male nor female” with respect to standing before God (Galatians 3:28); the gospel restores to both the dignity creation gave them.

Because every person bears God’s image, every person has a worth that no social position, ability, or failure can erase. James finds it incongruous to bless God and then curse “men, which are made after the similitude of God” (James 3:9). Sin has defaced the image without abolishing the dignity it confers, and in Christ that image is being restored “from glory to glory” (2 Corinthians 3:18).

wordNotes.term: זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה (zakhar uneqevah) — male and female
wordNotes.explanation: Two terms that designate sex, used also of the animals that entered the ark in pairs. Here they specify that ’adam, humankind, exists as man and woman. Jesus quotes the phrase in its Greek form, arsen kai thēly, to ground marriage in the Creator’s original design.

verses.bibleText: And God blessed them, and God said unto them, Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth, and subdue it: and have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over every living thing that moveth upon the earth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And God blessed them, and God said unto them.” The blessing of the fish and birds was spoken over them; this one is addressed to the man and woman. They can hear, understand, and respond. Here God speaks to human beings for the first time, and the relationship between Creator and creature begins as conversation. Humanity’s first experience is to receive blessing from God’s own lips.

The blessing includes fruitfulness: “Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth.” The English “replenish” has sometimes been taken to mean refilling an earth emptied by an earlier catastrophe. The Hebrew male’ simply means “fill,” the verb already used of the sea creatures filling the waters in verse 22. Nothing here suggests a former population. God intended the earth to be filled with families who would carry His image across the world, and children are presented as His gift (Psalm 127:3).

The blessing also includes a commission: “subdue it: and have dominion.” The verb kavash is strong; elsewhere it describes bringing land or people under control. In this setting, before sin, it means bringing the earth’s potential into use—cultivating, developing, and ordering it. Chapter 2 gives the concrete form: the man is placed in the garden “to dress it and to keep it” (2:15). Dominion is real authority, yet it is held by a servant of God who will give account, for the earth remains “the LORD’s” (Psalm 24:1).

The mandate frames human work as a calling from God, given before the fall and therefore good in itself. Sin will make labor painful and dominion distorted (3:17–19), but it does not cancel the commission. In Christ the redeemed are restored to their royal vocation, and Scripture anticipates the day when they will reign with Him in a renewed creation (Revelation 5:10; 22:5).

wordNotes.explanation: From kavash, “to subdue, bring under control.” It is used of the land of Canaan being subdued before Israel and of bringing people into subjection. In Genesis 1, set within blessing and before any sin, the sense is ordering and developing the earth for the purposes God intended, not plundering it.

From male’, “to be full, to fill.” In older English “replenish” simply meant “fill.” The verb gives no support to the idea of a previously inhabited earth; it is the same command spoken to the sea creatures in verse 22 and to Noah’s family after the flood.

verses.bibleText: And God said, Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed, which is upon the face of all the earth, and every tree, in the which is the fruit of a tree yielding seed; to you it shall be for meat.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed, which is upon the face of all the earth, and every tree, in the which is the fruit of a tree yielding seed; to you it shall be for meat.” In older English “meat” means food in general. God’s provision is generous. Having blessed and commissioned the man and woman, He sets before them the food He has prepared: seed-bearing plants, such as grains and legumes, and the fruit of trees, including nuts. These are the two kinds of vegetation described on the third day (vv. 11–12).

The original human diet involved no killing. Animals were placed under human dominion, but they were not given as food. Only after the flood does God say, “Every moving thing that liveth shall be meat for you; even as the green herb have I given you all things” (9:3), and even then the permission is bounded by the prohibition of eating blood and by the distinction between clean and unclean animals already known to Noah (7:2). The permission of chapter 9 is a concession to a changed world; the provision of chapter 1 reflects the Creator’s ideal.

The verse reverses the pattern of Israel’s neighbors. In Mesopotamian stories humans were made to feed the gods with offerings. In Genesis God feeds humanity. The Creator provides for His creatures before they have done anything for Him, a picture of grace from the first day of human life.

The diet of Eden carries an enduring lesson for health and stewardship. The foods God first chose for His children remain wholesome, and Scripture links the care of the body with the honor of God: “whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31). Isaiah’s vision of the new earth, where none shall “hurt nor destroy,” implies a return to the peace of the beginning (Isaiah 65:25).

wordNotes.term: הִנֵּה נָתַתִּי (hinneh natatti) — Behold, I have given
wordNotes.explanation: “Behold” draws attention to what follows, and the perfect verb “I have given” presents the gift as settled. The same verb of giving recurs when God permits animal food after the flood, so the two passages appear as successive gifts of the one Provider.

Literally “for food,” from the verb “to eat.” The King James “meat” reflects older English usage for any food. The phrase states the purpose of the plants God gave and recurs in verse 30 for the food of the animals.

verses.bibleText: And to every beast of the earth, and to every fowl of the air, and to every thing that creepeth upon the earth, wherein there is life, I have given every green herb for meat: and it was so.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The provision extends to every animal: “to every beast of the earth, and to every fowl of the air, and to every thing that creepeth upon the earth, wherein there is life, I have given every green herb for meat.” The phrase “wherein there is life” renders nefesh chayyah, the “living creature” of verses 20 and 24. Animals, birds, and creeping things alike receive green plants as their food.

The implication is striking. In the world as God first made it, animals did not prey on one another. Predation, suffering, and death had no place in the creation God called “very good.” Scripture traces their entrance to sin: the ground is cursed because of Adam (3:17), death enters the world through one man (Romans 5:12), and creation itself now “groaneth and travaileth in pain together” as it waits for redemption (Romans 8:20–22). The text does not explain how animal bodies and behavior changed, and humility is fitting there, but it does make clear that violence among creatures is a mark of a fallen world.

The prophets look forward to the reversal of that condition. Isaiah sees the wolf dwelling with the lamb and the lion eating straw like the ox, with a little child leading them, because “they shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain” (Isaiah 11:6–9; 65:25). The end of the story recovers the peace of its beginning.

“And it was so.” The arrangement stood. God’s care reaches every creature, and His provision for animals is part of His goodness; He “giveth to the beast his food, and to the young ravens which cry” (Psalm 147:9).

wordNotes.explanation: Yereq refers to green foliage, and with ‘esev it denotes green plants generally. After the flood God extends the permission for human food with an explicit comparison to “the green herb,” showing that this verse defined the original diet.

verses.bibleText: And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. And the evening and the morning were the sixth day.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good.” The seventh and final verdict surveys the whole. Earlier verdicts weighed individual works; this one embraces “every thing.” The word “behold” calls the reader to look with God, and the added “very” lifts the verdict to its highest point. With humanity in place, creation is complete and harmonious, each part fitted to the others and to the Creator’s purpose.

“Very good” rules out any thought that the world came from God’s hand flawed, violent, or unfinished. There was no sin, suffering, or death in it, and nothing in the creatures predisposed them to fall. When evil appears in chapter 3, it enters from outside, through the serpent’s deception and human disobedience. The verdict also stands against any account in which death and struggle over long ages were God’s chosen means of producing life. A process built on death could hardly be pronounced very good, and Scripture names death “the last enemy” (1 Corinthians 15:26). Paul affirms the abiding goodness of what God made: “every creature of God is good” (1 Timothy 4:4).

“And the evening and the morning were the sixth day.” In Hebrew this is the first day to receive the definite article—literally “the sixth day”—marking its climactic place. Six evening-and-morning days have now passed, and the creation week stands one day short of completion. The fourth commandment summarizes exactly this: “in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them is” (Exodus 20:11). The seventh day, when God rests, blesses, and sanctifies, follows directly (2:1–3).

The goodness of the first creation is the measure of what sin destroyed and of what God will restore. Christ, through whom all things were made, came to redeem a fallen world, and He promises a new heaven and a new earth where “there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying” (Revelation 21:1–5). The verdict of the sixth day is more than a memory; it is a pledge of the world to come.

wordNotes.explanation: Me’od intensifies tov, so the closing verdict exceeds those of the earlier days. It is the only place in the chapter where the evaluation is strengthened and where it covers the whole creation at once. The phrase expresses complete approval: nothing was lacking, defective, or out of place.

wordNotes.term: יוֹם הַשִּׁשִּׁי (yom hashshishi) — the sixth day
wordNotes.explanation: The only one of the six working days whose number carries the definite article, singling it out as the culmination of God’s work. The seventh day that follows also carries the article, and together the two close the creation week. The manna narrative later makes “the sixth day” the day of preparation for the Sabbath.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: What changes in the way we see ourselves and the world when the first fact Scripture teaches is that God was there before anything else?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: The one true God created the heavens and the earth by His word in six days, made everything good, and crowned His work with humanity made in His image to know Him, reflect Him, and care for His world.
discussionQuestions: How does the repeated phrase “And God said” shape our understanding of God’s power and of the authority of His word?
Why does the text close each day with “the evening and the morning,” and how does Exodus 20:11 confirm what kind of days these were?
What does it mean that every human being, male and female, bears God’s image, and how should that govern the way we treat others?
What does the pattern of forming and then filling reveal about God’s purpose and care?
What does the plant diet of verses 29–30 suggest about God’s design for a world without death?
commonMisunderstandings: The days of Genesis 1 are not long ages; the evening-and-morning refrain, the numbered sequence, and the fourth commandment describe ordinary days.
Verse 2 does not describe a ruined former world; Scripture leaves no room for an age of judgment and death between verses 1 and 2.
Dominion is not a license to exploit; it is royal stewardship under God, exercised for the good of what is ruled.
The plural “Let us” is not a council of lesser gods; Scripture as a whole reveals the Father, the Son, and the Spirit at work in creation.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep the Creator at the center: the chapter is first about who God is and what His word accomplishes, and only then about the world and the people He made good.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Worship the Creator who spoke light into darkness, receive your life as His gift, and let the God who made you in His image renew that image in you through Jesus Christ.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: God created all things by His word in six days, and the same Creator restores His image in fallen people through Christ.
flow: God existed before all things and created the heavens and the earth by His word.
He made the world in six real days, and everything He made was very good.
Human beings were made in His image to know Him, reflect His character, and care for His world.
Sin has marred that image, but the Word through whom all things were made became flesh to restore it.
The God who said “Let there be light” can shine into a darkened heart and make a person new.
simpleIllustrations: A well-built house says something about its builder; a world lit, ordered, and stocked for life speaks of a Maker who is both wise and kind.
A coin bears the image of its ruler and is rendered to him (Matthew 22:20-21); people bear God’s image and belong to Him.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you acknowledge the Creator as your God and let Him, through Christ, renew His image in you?
cautions: Present the account as true history while treating those who hold other views with courtesy; let the text do its own persuading.
Do not reduce the image of God to a single faculty such as reason; it embraces the whole person.
Do not treat the chapter as a technical science manual; its purpose is to reveal the Creator, and its statements remain trustworthy.

reflectionQuestions: Do I begin my days, plans, and decisions with God, as Scripture begins with Him?
Where do I need the Creator to speak light into darkness in my own life?
How does knowing that every person bears God’s image change the way I speak about and treat others?
How am I caring for the part of God’s creation that has been entrusted to me?
Do I trust the word that created the world to accomplish what it promises in me?
